question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?
title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) explained
direct_answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) states that objects of a subclass should be replaceable for objects of their superclass without breaking the program. If class B extends class A, anywhere you use an A object you should be able to use a B object and get the same correct behavior — no surprises, no exceptions.

sections.title: Why LSP Matters for Polymorphism
sections.content: The **Liskov Substitution Principle** is the L in SOLID. It says that **subclasses must be substitutable for their parent classes** without altering the correctness of the program. Named after Barbara Liskov, this principle ensures that **polymorphism works safely** in production code. Think of it like a promise: if a method accepts a `Vehicle` parameter, you should be able to pass a `Car` or `Truck` and the method should work correctly without knowing which specific subclass it received. The key insight is that **inheritance is not just about code reuse** — it's about creating **behavioral contracts** that subtypes must honor. When LSP is violated, you get **runtime surprises**: exceptions thrown, incorrect results, or broken invariants. A common analogy: if you hire a substitute teacher, students shouldn't notice any difference in how the class runs. The substitute must fulfill the same role, same expectations, same outcomes. In Java code, this means **overridden methods must not weaken preconditions, strengthen postconditions, or throw new checked exceptions** that the parent didn't declare.

sections.title: LSP Violation with Rectangle and Square
Key Points
content: **Behavioral substitutability**: subclass objects must work everywhere parent objects work without breaking correctness
**Contract preservation**: overridden methods cannot weaken preconditions (require more) or strengthen postconditions (promise less)
**Exception compatibility**: subclasses cannot throw new checked exceptions that the parent method didn't declare
**Invariant maintenance**: class invariants that hold for the parent must also hold for the subclass across all operations
**Compile-time vs runtime**: code that compiles is not enough — LSP is about runtime behavioral correctness
**Rectangle-Square problem**: classic example where mathematical is-a relationship does not translate to OOP inheritance
**Polymorphism safety**: LSP is what makes polymorphism reliable — without it, you need runtime type checks everywhere

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Liskov Substitution Principle says that a subclass must be able to replace its parent class without breaking the program. It's the L in SOLID. Let me explain what that means in practice. If I have a method that accepts a Vehicle parameter, I should be able to pass it a Car or a Truck, and the method should work correctly without knowing which specific subclass it got. The classic violation example is Rectangle and Square. Mathematically, a square is a rectangle. But in code, if Square extends Rectangle, you run into problems. Say Rectangle has setWidth and setHeight methods that work independently. If I write code that sets width to five and height to four, I expect the area to be twenty. But if you pass in a Square object, setting width also changes height because a square's sides must be equal. Now the area is sixteen, and my code breaks. That's an LSP violation. The subclass changed the expected behavior. A common mistake freshers make is thinking that if the code compiles, LSP is satisfied. But LSP is about runtime behavior, not just types. If your subclass throws UnsupportedOperationException or returns unexpected values, you've violated LSP even though it compiles. The key takeaway is that inheritance should be based on behavioral compatibility, not just real-world relationships. Just because something is-a something in the real world doesn't mean it should extend it in code.

question: How do you fix a Liskov Substitution Principle violation?
title: Fixing LSP violations — composition vs inheritance
direct_answer: The usual fix is to not use inheritance where the subclass cannot truly substitute the parent. Instead, use a common interface without the problematic shared state, or use composition. If Square and Rectangle have incompatible behavior, they should both implement a Shape interface independently rather than one extending the other.

sections.title: Three Strategies to Fix LSP Violations
sections.content: When you discover an **LSP violation**, the solution is almost never to force the inheritance to work. The core fix is to **stop using inheritance** where behavioral substitution fails. There are three main strategies: **(1) extract a common interface** — remove the problematic parent class and have both types implement a shared interface with only the operations they can both truly support; **(2) use composition** — instead of extending, have one class contain the other as a field and delegate selectively; **(3) eliminate the subclass** — if the types really are different behaviors, make them separate classes with no inheritance relationship. The Rectangle-Square problem is fixed by having both implement a `Shape` interface with just `area()` and `draw()` methods — no setters. Neither extends the other. This aligns with the principle **favor composition over inheritance**. Inheritance creates tight coupling and rigid contracts. Composition gives you flexibility to pick which behaviors to reuse without inheriting the entire contract. Many LSP violations come from **premature generalization** — assuming that because two things share some attributes they should share a class hierarchy.

sections.title: Fixing Rectangle-Square with Interface
Key Points
content: **Extract interface**: replace parent class with a shared interface containing only operations both types can genuinely support
**Composition over inheritance**: use a has-a relationship instead of is-a when behavioral substitution fails
**Remove setters**: many LSP violations come from mutable state — immutable objects with constructor parameters avoid this
**Separate classes**: if types have fundamentally different behaviors, don't force them into a hierarchy at all
**No UnsupportedOperationException**: throwing this in an override is itself an LSP violation, not a fix
**Design by capability**: group types by what they can do (interface), not by what they are (taxonomy)
**Favor immutability**: using records or final fields eliminates many LSP violation scenarios

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you find an LSP violation, the fix is usually to stop using inheritance. Let me walk through the main approach. Take the Rectangle-Square problem. The violation happens because Square can't properly substitute Rectangle — setting width and height independently doesn't make sense for a square. The fix is to not have Square extend Rectangle at all. Instead, create a Shape interface with just the methods both types can truly support, like area and draw. Rectangle and Square both implement Shape independently. Rectangle keeps its setWidth and setHeight methods, and Square has a single setSide method. Now there's no inheritance, so there's no substitution to violate. Another strategy is composition. If you have a class that can't fully substitute its parent, make it contain the parent as a field instead of extending it. Then delegate only the methods that make sense. This is the favor composition over inheritance principle. A common mistake is trying to fix LSP by throwing UnsupportedOperationException in the subclass methods that don't work. That's not a fix, that's actually another LSP violation. You're still breaking the contract at runtime. The real lesson is that inheritance should be rare. Use it only when you have true behavioral substitution. Most of the time, interfaces and composition are safer choices. In Spring Boot apps, you'll see this pattern everywhere — services implement interfaces, and they compose repositories rather than extending base classes.

question: What does throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass mean for LSP?
title: UnsupportedOperationException and LSP violation
direct_answer: Throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass method is an LSP violation. It means the subclass cannot fulfill the contract of the parent — code that calls that method on the parent type will break at runtime when given the subclass. A real-world example is Collections.unmodifiableList() — calling add() throws, which surprises callers.

sections.title: Why Throwing UnsupportedOperationException Violates LSP
sections.content: When a subclass overrides a method to **throw UnsupportedOperationException**, it's explicitly saying "I cannot do what my parent promised." This is a **runtime LSP violation**. The parent class or interface established a **contract** — the method exists, it has a signature, and callers expect it to work. When the subclass throws this exception, **code written against the parent type will fail** when it receives the subclass instance. It compiles fine, but **blows up at runtime**. The Java Collections Framework has famous examples of this. `Collections.unmodifiableList()` wraps an ArrayList in a view that throws `UnsupportedOperationException` on any mutation method like `add()` or `remove()`. Technically it implements the `List` interface, but it **violates the List contract** because List's Javadoc says these methods should work. This is a **pragmatic trade-off** the JDK makes for immutability, but it's still an LSP violation. In interview terms, this shows that **passing the compiler is not the same as honoring a behavioral contract**. If your class can't support an operation, **don't inherit or implement that interface** — use a different abstraction.

sections.title: UnsupportedOperationException LSP Violation
Key Points
content: **Runtime failure**: throwing UnsupportedOperationException breaks polymorphism at runtime, not compile time
**Contract violation**: the parent type promised the method works — the subclass breaks that promise
**Collections API example**: Collections.unmodifiableList is a pragmatic but real LSP violation in the JDK
**Not a workaround**: catching UnsupportedOperationException everywhere defeats polymorphism and adds fragility
**Interface segregation**: if a class can't support an operation, split the interface so it doesn't have to implement it
**Fail-fast is not LSP-safe**: throwing immediately is better than silent corruption, but neither is substitutable
**Alternative design**: use Optional return types, separate interfaces, or composition to avoid unsupported methods

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Throwing UnsupportedOperationException in a subclass method is an LSP violation. Here's why. When a subclass inherits or implements a method, it's making a promise to fulfill that contract. If it throws UnsupportedOperationException instead, it's breaking that promise at runtime. Code that works with the parent type will fail when it gets the subclass. Let me give you a concrete example. Say you have a PaymentProcessor interface with processPayment and refundPayment methods. CreditCardProcessor implements both. But GiftCardProcessor can't do refunds, so it throws UnsupportedOperationException in the refundPayment method. Now imagine a handleReturn method that takes a PaymentProcessor and calls refundPayment. It works fine with CreditCardProcessor, but crashes with GiftCardProcessor. That's an LSP violation. The Java Collections API has real examples of this. Collections.unmodifiableList wraps a list and throws UnsupportedOperationException on methods like add and remove. It implements the List interface, but it violates the List contract because those methods are supposed to work. This is a pragmatic trade-off the JDK makes for immutability, but it's still technically an LSP violation. The key lesson is that you can't just catch UnsupportedOperationException everywhere. That defeats the whole point of polymorphism. If a class can't support an operation, it shouldn't implement that interface. Use interface segregation instead — split the interface into smaller pieces so each class only implements what it can truly support.

sections.title: LSP as Contract Enforcement
sections.content: At its core, **LSP is about honoring behavioral contracts**. When you write a class or interface, you establish **expectations** — not just the method signatures, but the **semantics**: what inputs are valid (preconditions), what outputs you guarantee (postconditions), and what state stays consistent (invariants). A subclass or implementation must **uphold these contracts**. **Design by Contract**, formalized by Bertrand Meyer, makes this explicit: every method has a **precondition** (what must be true before calling), a **postcondition** (what must be true after), and **class invariants** (what must always be true). LSP says a subclass **cannot strengthen preconditions** (require more from callers), **cannot weaken postconditions** (promise less in return), and must **maintain all invariants**. For example, if a parent method accepts any positive integer, the subclass can't suddenly require it to be even — that strengthens the precondition and breaks LSP. This applies equally to **interface implementations**, not just class inheritance. If a Spring `@Repository` interface declares `findById(Long id)` returns `Optional<Customer>`, an implementation that throws `IllegalArgumentException` for null id violates the contract if the interface didn't specify that precondition. LSP is the **runtime enforcement** of these contracts through polymorphism.

sections.title: LSP Contract Violation Example
Key Points
content: **Design by Contract**: formal framework with preconditions (input requirements), postconditions (output guarantees), and invariants (persistent state rules)
**Precondition rule**: subclasses cannot require more (strengthen) — they must accept at least what the parent accepts
**Postcondition rule**: subclasses cannot promise less (weaken) — they must deliver at least what the parent delivers
**Invariant preservation**: class-level rules that hold true across all operations must remain true in subclasses
**Interface implementations**: LSP applies to interface implementations just as much as class inheritance
**Semantic compatibility**: matching method signatures is not enough — the behavior must match expectations
**Spring contracts**: repository interfaces, service layers, and REST controllers all establish contracts that implementations must honor

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: LSP is fundamentally about honoring contracts. Let me explain what that means. When you create a class or interface, you're not just defining method signatures. You're establishing a behavioral contract. That includes preconditions, which are what must be true before you call a method. Postconditions, which are what the method guarantees after it runs. And invariants, which are things that must always stay true about the object's state. A subclass or implementation must honor all of these. The formal term for this is Design by Contract. Here's the key rule. A subclass cannot strengthen preconditions. That means it can't require more from callers than the parent did. For example, if the parent method accepts any positive number, the subclass can't suddenly demand that it be even. That would break code that passes odd numbers to the parent type. Similarly, a subclass cannot weaken postconditions. It has to deliver at least what the parent promised. This applies to interfaces too, not just inheritance. If a Spring repository interface says findById accepts any Long and returns an Optional, an implementation that throws IllegalArgumentException for null violates the contract. Even though it compiles, it breaks LSP. In a Spring Boot app, you see this everywhere. Service interfaces establish contracts about transactional behavior, exception handling, and return types. Implementations must honor those contracts fully. If they don't, client code that depends on the interface will break when it gets a specific implementation. That's why LSP matters in real production systems.

sections.title: Taxonomy vs Behavior in Inheritance
sections.content: **is-a** describes a **taxonomic relationship** — how we classify things in the real world or mathematics. A square is-a rectangle by definition: all sides equal, all angles ninety degrees. A penguin is-a bird by taxonomy. **behaves-like-a** describes **behavioral substitutability** — whether one type can replace another in code without breaking functionality. This is what **LSP requires**. The critical insight for OOP: **real-world taxonomy does not automatically translate to code inheritance**. A square is mathematically a rectangle, but in code a Square class often cannot substitute a Rectangle class because of **behavioral incompatibility**. Similarly, a penguin is biologically a bird, but if your Bird class has a `fly()` method, Penguin breaks that contract. The lesson: **inheritance should be driven by behavioral contracts, not domain vocabulary**. If two classes share a name relationship in English but have different operation sets or constraints, they should **not use inheritance**. Use composition or separate interfaces instead. This is why **favor composition over inheritance** is sound advice — composition lets you reuse code without making rigid substitutability promises you can't keep.

rows: Square cannot behave-like-a Rectangle with independent width/height setters
Penguin cannot behave-like-a Bird if Bird has fly method
Only when subclass can fully substitute parent in all use cases

sections.title: When to Use Inheritance Based on Behavior
sections.content: Use inheritance **only when the subclass can fully substitute the parent** in all realistic use cases. Ask: will any code that works with the parent type still work correctly with the subclass? Can the subclass honor all preconditions, postconditions, and invariants? If the answer is yes, inheritance is safe. If no, use a **common interface** or **composition**. For the Rectangle-Square problem, the behavioral test fails: code that independently sets width and height breaks with Square. So don't use inheritance — make both implement a Shape interface with just `area()` and `draw()`. For Penguin-Bird, if Bird has a `fly()` method, Penguin fails the behavioral test. Solution: extract a `WalkingAnimal` or `Animal` interface without `fly()`, and have a separate `FlyingBird` interface that only flying birds implement. The rule of thumb: **if you find yourself throwing UnsupportedOperationException or adding runtime type checks (instanceof), your inheritance is wrong**. That's a symptom of taxonomic inheritance instead of behavioral inheritance. Real-world taxonomy is a trap — it feels intuitive but breaks at runtime.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **is-a is taxonomic**: describes real-world or mathematical classification, not code inheritance suitability
**behaves-like-a is LSP**: requires full behavioral substitutability in all use cases
**Taxonomy trap**: using domain vocabulary to drive inheritance leads to LSP violations
**Square-Rectangle**: classic example where mathematical is-a fails behavioral substitutability
**Penguin-Bird**: another example where biological taxonomy doesn't translate to code hierarchy
**Favor composition**: when is-a doesn't align with behaves-like-a, use composition or interfaces
**Behavioral contracts**: inheritance decisions should be based on method contracts, not English definitions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between is-a and behaves-like-a is critical for understanding when to use inheritance. is-a is a taxonomic relationship. It's how we classify things in the real world or math. A square is-a rectangle mathematically because it meets the definition. A penguin is-a bird biologically. behaves-like-a is the LSP requirement. It asks whether one type can substitute another in code without breaking anything. This is what matters for inheritance. Here's the key insight. Real-world taxonomy doesn't automatically translate to code inheritance. A square is mathematically a rectangle, but in code, a Square class usually can't substitute a Rectangle class. Why? Because Rectangle typically has setWidth and setHeight methods that work independently. If you pass a Square to code that sets width to five and height to four, it breaks. The square can't maintain independent dimensions. That's a behavioral incompatibility even though taxonomically it's valid. Same with penguin and bird. If your Bird class has a fly method, Penguin breaks that contract. It can't fly. So even though biologically a penguin is a bird, in code Penguin shouldn't extend Bird if Bird has flight behavior. The lesson is that inheritance should be driven by behavioral contracts, not domain vocabulary. Don't inherit just because two things have a real-world is-a relationship. Only inherit when the subclass can truly substitute the parent in all use cases. If you can't, use a common interface or composition instead. That's why favor composition over inheritance is such strong advice. Composition gives you flexibility without forcing behavioral substitution promises you can't keep.
